findings.summary: The four-stream arm's premise -- that production really sees four RunKeys -- is still unguarded in this file, and one character silently voids half the test
findings.detail: MEASURED. Changing `runs.put(new RunKey(DedupFixtures.A, i), 2)` to `new RunKey(DedupFixtures.A, 0)` makes the loop write one key four times, so forwardedCommitCost(4) becomes a second copy of forwardedCommitCost(1). With that one-character edit in place AND the per-RunKey lease read reinstated in RemoteSequencer.commitAll, the whole sequencer module is 497/497 GREEN -- the exact mutation this task exists to kill survives, and both whole-record assertions still pass because both arms now measure one stream. The whole-record assertion does not close this: it compares atOne and atFour to the same literal, so a degraded fixture makes them agree trivially. No gate sees it either -- check-test-integrity flags weakened ASSERTIONS beside a production change, and this is a fixture edit with no assertion touched. One line closes it, e.g. `assertThat(runs).hasSize(streams)` before the commit, or asserting the request's recordCounts().size(). Minor rather than major because it takes a test-side edit to trigger, not a production regression, and the test as staged kills every mutation measured.
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED at 497/497 green: change `runs.put(new RunKey(DedupFixtures.A, i), 2)` to `new RunKey(DedupFixtures.A, 0)` (a test-side edit no gate flags, since no assertion changes) AND reinstate the per-RunKey lease read in RemoteSequencer.commitAll. The whole sequencer module stays green -- the four-stream arm has silently become a second one-stream arm, both record assertions still pass, and the per-stream shape non-negotiable 6 forbids by name is back with the test reporting it pinned.

findings.summary: The four surviving reads()/puts() accessor assertions cannot fail -- they are dead, and SPEC.md:305 names exactly those as the self-enforcing sites
findings.detail: Lines 134-144 are unreachable-on-failure by construction: the two `isEqualTo(new StoreCounts(1,2,0,1,0))` assertions at :126 and :130 run first, so either delta is exactly that record (whence reads()==3 and delta().puts()==1 necessarily) or AssertJ throws and these four lines never execute. No mutation can make them fire. That is not itself a hole -- MEASURED: deleting ONLY the two record assertions and keeping these four leaves the per-RunKey LIST mutation surviving at 497/497 green, i.e. the record assertions carry all the falsifying power and these carry none. The consequence is documentary. The `Cost` javadoc at :150-158 says the accessors 'exist only to make the failure message readable', but they produce no failure message at all -- MEASURED under the per-RunKey lease read, the message an engineer actually sees is the atFour record one ('expected StoreCounts[puts=1, gets=2, ...] but was [puts=1, gets=5, ...]'), and the explanatory :137 message naming the 6 is never reached. Worse, SPEC.md:305 says that when M5.6g lands 'FOUR sites change ... BOTH `isEqualTo(3L)` values ... Only the assertion values are self-enforcing' -- naming the two DEAD assertions and omitting the two live `StoreCounts` records, which is the opposite of what the test's own javadoc at :115 says ('both expected StoreCounts'). Failure scenario: M5.6g's author follows the SPEC, edits both `isEqualTo(3L)` to `1L`, leaves the records at (1,2,0,1,0). Not silent -- the record assertion reds -- but the author was pointed at the wrong sites and told the dead ones are the self-enforcing ones. Either delete the accessors and `Cost.reads()`, or make the SPEC name the records.
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED at 497/497 green: delete ONLY the two `isEqualTo(new StoreCounts(1,2,0,1,0))` lines at :126 and :130, keep the four accessor assertions, and add a per-RunKey LIST beyond the first in RemoteSequencer.commitAll -- a LIST per stream per flush, which cost.md R2 and R15 forbid outright. Module green. The converse is what makes the accessors dead: no mutation can reach them while the records stand, so `Cost.reads()`'s stated purpose (a readable failure message) never happens -- under the per-RunKey lease read the message seen is the atFour record's `gets=5`, not :137's explanation of the 6. Documentary consequence: an M5.6g author following SPEC.md:305's 'BOTH `isEqualTo(3L)` values ... Only the assertion values are self-enforcing' edits the two assertions that constrain nothing and leaves the two that do.

findings.summary: The same cost cell prices a SECOND number -- 'FOUR when the lease has moved' -- and nothing counts it; two extra lease GETs on the refusal arm survive the module
findings.detail: MEASURED: inserting two extra `currentLease()` calls in RemoteSequencer.commitAll's `NotTheLeaseholderException` arm (making the refusal path 6 requests instead of 4) leaves the sequencer module 497/497 GREEN. The new test brackets only the non-refusal path, and the only other counting test on this path, RemoteSequencerTest.forwardingAddsNoOBJECTSTOREWriteOfItsOwn, counts PUTs on the non-refusal path too. The commit does not misstate this -- the right-hand cell scopes 'PINNED (M5.33)' to the +3 and names the test -- so this is a neighbouring unpinned number rather than a false claim, and it is pre-existing rather than created here. Raised because it is the same defect shape the task was opened for: a number written into the cost table that no assertion constrains, one clause away from the one that now is. Worth a backlog row rather than a fix in this commit.
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION, MEASURED at 497/497 green: insert two extra `currentLease()` calls before `Lease moved = currentLease();` in RemoteSequencer.commitAll's `NotTheLeaseholderException` arm, taking the refusal path from the 4 store requests SPEC.md:305 prices to 6. Nothing in the module reds. A later change that re-reads the lease again on refusal -- or M5.6g touching that arm -- lands a 50% cost increase on the failover path with the cost table still reading FOUR and the neighbouring cell reading PINNED.

findings.summary: The renewer is parked but the 60 s CHECKPOINT ticker is still live inside the measured window -- the same flake class, 20x wider
findings.detail: The 5-arg LocalSequencer.start the fixture calls delegates to the 7-arg one with `CheckpointWriter.sleepFor(CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL)` = 60 s, so the leader still runs a real-clock timer whose tick issues TWO PUTs (putIfAbsent of the checkpoint plus put of the pointer) -- and `dirty` is already set by the priming `leader.commit(...)` at :179, so the tick would not early-return. A >=60 s stall between pod construction and the `after` read turns the exact pins into a flake giving puts=3, which is the failure mode the parked renewer comment at :60-64 was written for, one order of magnitude further out. Concretely: build.md's own WSL2 session-suspend case. Strictly lower probability than the 3 s renewer that was fixed, and the fix is available in the same idiom -- the package-private 7-arg start takes a CheckpointWriter.Ticker. Raised so the comment at :60 does not read as 'every clock in this window is parked' when one is not.
findings.failure_scenario: CONCRETE FAILURE SCENARIO, not a mutation: the leader's CheckpointWriter thread is started by the 5-arg `LocalSequencer.start` with the shipped 60 s `CheckpointWriter.sleepFor(CHECKPOINT_INTERVAL)`, and `dirty` is already true from the priming commit at :179, so a tick landing between `var before = store.counts();` and `var after = store.counts();` issues two PUTs and the test reds with puts=3 against an expected 1. This is the same failure the parked renewer at :60-64 was written to remove -- MEASURED there: restoring the 4-arg start and stalling 4 s inside the window reds the test; with the renewer parked the same 4 s stall is green. The checkpoint ticker needs a >=60 s stall instead, which build.md's WSL2 session-suspend case supplies. The 7-arg package-private `start` already takes a CheckpointWriter.Ticker, so the same idiom closes it.
